doc.title: Donn Andre interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 6, 2009

title: Learning tunes off records and from Paul Parker
summary: Tunes came from records and Paul Parker's chording, with songs already in their heads.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: So when you came here and you got into the situation you were playing with in a rehearsal, how did you learn the songs?

Mainly off the records. Or, as happens, somebody might know the melody — well Paul Parker would chord it for us and he’d say this is how it goes, and we’d try and get it and he’d say no, no, that’s wrong, you know, so we’d learn it that way. But for some reason, and I think it’s because of this affinity for music that we all had, and listening to records even before we were in a band, that the tunes were up here. They were already in our heads for some reason. You know. And Em would call, let’s do “Nobody’s Sweetheart Now,” you know, we’d just launch into it. And Mike knew the tune and off we went. I was amazed frequently about how these tunes just sort of came out. And as I said, I did a lot of — not folk — oh yeah, folk songs, sing-a-longs, you know, the old tunes from the 20s and the 30s and 40s. Popular hits like “By the Light of the Silvery Moon” or that stuff. Of course we didn’t play that but we did play some other tunes that lodged in my brain somehow.
